title: Stronger legs, same fall risk
objective: Selecting and interpreting outcome measures across impairment, activity and participation in older adults

brief.situation: 11:00 at Mr. Petrov's home. You are the home health physical therapist. Mr. Petrov, 79, fell in the street 3 months ago. This is the last planned visit of an 8-week falls program. The referral says 'discharge when strength improves', and his sit-to-stand strength has clearly improved. His daughter says he still won't go to the shops or church on his own.
handover: At intake: gait speed 0.62 m/s, high fear of falling on the short FES-I, five sit-to-stands in 19 seconds.
Agency policy: discharge decisions use the program's outcome set and are reported to the referring physician.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

parts.modelAnswer: No. His legs are stronger, but he still walks under 0.8 m/s, he's still scared of falling, and he won't go out on his own.

scoring.modelReasoning: Choose outcome measures across impairment (sit-to-stand), activity (gait speed) and participation (getting to church and the shops), and read them together. A strength gain does not meet falls-prevention goals when gait speed is still below 0.8 m/s, which flags risk, and fear of falling remains high. Continue care on those targets and report the full set.
